profile.feeling: Spicy warmth: ginger tea in winter, Asian cooking and the trendy ginger shot.

senses.def: ginger (the plant and its spicy rhizome)

examples.text: Für den Tee reibe ich ein Stück frischen Ingwer.
examples.tr: For the tea I grate a piece of fresh ginger.

examples.text: Ingwer schmeckt würzig und leicht scharf.
examples.tr: Ginger tastes spicy and slightly hot.

examples.text: Gegen Übelkeit trinkt sie gern Ingwertee.
examples.tr: She likes to drink ginger tea against nausea.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; Ingber and Imber are obsolete dialect forms (Wiktionary).

etymology.text: From Middle High German ingewer, ingeber, from Old High German ingiber, gingiber, gingibero, from Proto-West Germanic *gingiberō; ultimately (via Late Latin gingiber, Latin zingiberi, Ancient Greek ζιγγίβερις and Prakrit siṃgivera) from Old Tamil iñcivēr.

funFacts: English ginger, Arabic زَنْجَبِيل (zanjabīl) and Turkish zencefil go back to the same ancient word from South India as German Ingwer.
pitfalls: Masculine: der Ingwer. The plural (die Ingwer) is rare; as food it is uncountable: Ich kaufe Ingwer, ein Stück Ingwer.
subtleties: One piece of the root is usually called eine Ingwerknolle or ein Stück Ingwer, although botanically it is a rhizome, not a root.

profile.feeling: Aniseed scent, crunchy white bulbs, and fennel tea for babies.

senses.def: fennel (the plant; as a vegetable, its white bulb)

examples.text: Den Fenchel in dünne Scheiben schneiden und mit Orangen servieren.
examples.tr: Cut the fennel into thin slices and serve with oranges.

examples.text: Der Fenchel riecht ein bisschen nach Anis.
examples.tr: The fennel smells a little of aniseed.

examples.text: Fencheltee hilft bei Bauchschmerzen, sagt meine Oma.
examples.tr: Fennel tea helps with stomach ache, my grandma says.

synonyms.nuance: the bulb fennel, as opposed to the herb and the seeds

etymology.text: Ultimately from Latin fēnuculum.

funFacts: Ancient Greek μάραθον meant fennel – the battlefield of Marathon was a “place of fennel”, and Modern Greek still says μάραθο.
pitfalls: The plural looks like the singular: ein Fenchel, zwei Fenchel; only the dative plural adds -n (mit Fencheln).
subtleties: Fenchel can mean the vegetable bulb or the spice (the seeds). Gemüsefenchel or Knollenfenchel is the bulb, Fenchelsamen the seeds.

profile.feeling: Tropical staple food: starchy roots, tapioca and Brazilian or African cooking.

senses.def: cassava, manioc (the plant and its starchy root)

examples.text: In Brasilien ist Maniok ein wichtiges Grundnahrungsmittel.
examples.tr: In Brazil cassava is an important staple food.

examples.text: Roher Maniok ist giftig, deshalb muss man ihn immer kochen.
examples.tr: Raw cassava is poisonous, so you always have to cook it.

examples.text: Aus Maniok macht man Tapioka.
examples.tr: Tapioca is made from cassava.

synonyms.nuance: used in agriculture and development contexts; also spelled Cassava

etymology.text: Like English manioc (Wiktionary): from French manioc, through Portuguese mandioca, ultimately from Old Tupi mani’oka.

funFacts: The tapioca pearls in bubble tea are made from cassava starch.
pitfalls: No plural: Maniok is uncountable; one root is eine Maniokwurzel or eine Maniokknolle.
Masculine: der Maniok.
subtleties: In recipes you also meet Cassava (from Taíno via Spanish) and the Spanish name Yuca – all for the same root.

profile.feeling: A German passion: the white-asparagus season in spring, with potatoes, ham and hollandaise.

senses.def: asparagus (the plant and its edible shoots)

examples.text: Im Mai essen wir fast jeden Tag Spargel mit Kartoffeln und Sauce hollandaise.
examples.tr: In May we eat asparagus with potatoes and hollandaise sauce almost every day.

examples.text: Weißer Spargel wächst unter der Erde und bleibt deshalb hell.
examples.tr: White asparagus grows under the soil and therefore stays pale.

examples.text: Kannst du schon mal den Spargel schälen?
examples.tr: Can you start peeling the asparagus?

phrases.meaning: when the cherries are ripe (late June), the asparagus season is over

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; kinds are named weißer Spargel or Bleichspargel (white) and grüner Spargel (green).

etymology.text: From 15th-century Middle High German sparge, spargen, sparges, from Medieval Latin sparagus, asparagus, in part through Italian sparago; the ending -el (16th c.) probably after plant names such as Kerbel and Kümmel.

funFacts: The German asparagus season traditionally ends on 24 June, St John’s Day (Johannistag).
Greek σπαράγγι, English asparagus and German Spargel all go back to Latin asparagus, from Greek ἀσπάραγος.
pitfalls: Usually uncountable: Ich esse gern Spargel. Plural die Spargel (also Spargeln), dative mit Spargeln.
Standard German says der Spargel; in the south some speakers say die Spargel.
subtleties: Germans traditionally prefer white asparagus (Bleichspargel); green asparagus became common only in recent decades.

profile.feeling: Exotic and tropical: a starchy tuber from Asian and Pacific cooking.

senses.def: taro (the plant and its starchy corm)

examples.text: Taro muss man immer gut kochen, roh kratzt er im Hals.
examples.tr: Taro must always be cooked well; raw, it scratches your throat.

examples.text: Auf Hawaii macht man aus Taro einen Brei namens Poi.
examples.tr: In Hawaii a paste called poi is made from taro.

examples.text: Im Asialaden gibt es frische Taros.
examples.tr: There are fresh taros at the Asian shop.

etymology.text: From a Polynesian language (Duden); compare Māori taro, the source of English taro (Wiktionary).

funFacts: In Cyprus taro is κολοκάσι (kolokasi), from Ancient Greek κολοκάσιον; Arabic قُلْقَاس (qulqās) comes from the same Greek word.
pitfalls: Masculine: der Taro, des Taros, plural die Taros.
Raw taro irritates the mouth and throat (calcium oxalate crystals); always cook it.
subtleties: In German Taro normally means the starchy corm; the large leaves are eaten too, but are rarely sold in Germany.

profile.feeling: Asian cuisine and the sacred lotus flower; crunchy slices with a pattern of holes.

senses.def: lotus root (the edible rhizome of the lotus)

examples.text: Die Lotuswurzel hat innen viele Löcher.
examples.tr: The lotus root has many holes inside.

examples.text: In Scheiben geschnitten sehen Lotuswurzeln wie kleine Räder aus.
examples.tr: Cut into slices, lotus roots look like little wheels.

examples.text: Im Asialaden kaufe ich Lotuswurzel für eine Suppe.
examples.tr: I buy lotus root for a soup at the Asian shop.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; Lotoswurzel (from the variant Lotos) is a rarer spelling of the same word.

etymology.text: Lotus (“lotus”, variant of Lotos, borrowed from Latin lotos, from Ancient Greek λωτός) + Wurzel (“root”, from Old High German wurzala).

funFacts: Botanically it is not a root but the underground stem (rhizome) of the lotus; Chinese calls it 莲藕 (lián’ǒu).
pitfalls: Feminine because the last part, Wurzel, is feminine: die Lotuswurzel, plural die Lotuswurzeln.
subtleties: The lotus is a sacred flower in Buddhism and Hinduism, so the word can sound exotic or spiritual to German ears.

profile.feeling: Yellow meadows in spring, blowing on seed heads as a child – and bitter wild salad.

senses.def: dandelion (the plant; its young leaves are eaten as greens)
tooth of a lion (literal)

examples.text: Im Frühling sammeln wir jungen Löwenzahn für den Salat.
examples.tr: In spring we gather young dandelion for the salad.

examples.text: Die Wiese ist voller Löwenzahn.
examples.tr: The meadow is full of dandelions.

examples.text: Junge Löwenzahnblätter schmecken leicht bitter.
examples.tr: Young dandelion leaves taste slightly bitter.

synonyms.nuance: the round white seed head (“blow-flower”); children also use it for the whole plant

etymology.text: In the literal sense inherited from Middle High German lewenzan, Löwe (“lion”) + -n- + Zahn (“tooth”). The botanical sense is a 16th-century calque of Latin dēns leōnis, whence also English dandelion.

funFacts: Löwenzahn is also the name of a long-running German children’s TV programme (ZDF, since 1981).
English dandelion comes from French dent-de-lion, the same “lion’s tooth” image.
pitfalls: Plural Löwenzähne (several plants); the greens are uncountable: Ich esse gern Löwenzahn.
subtleties: The name comes from the jagged, tooth-like leaves; the white seed head is called Pusteblume.

profile.feeling: Old-fashioned, rustic root vegetable, now rediscovered by regional cooks.

senses.def: turnip (the white root of Brassica rapa)

examples.text: Die Speiserübe ist innen weiß und schmeckt mild.
examples.tr: The turnip is white inside and tastes mild.

examples.text: Teltower Rübchen sind kleine Speiserüben aus Brandenburg.
examples.tr: Teltow turnips are small turnips from Brandenburg.

examples.text: Im Herbst kocht sie eine Suppe aus Speiserüben und Kartoffeln.
examples.tr: In autumn she cooks a soup of turnips and potatoes.

synonyms.nuance: everyday description, after the white flesh
the Swiss word for the (autumn) turnip

etymology.text: From Speise (“food”) + Rübe (“beet, turnip”); Rübe is from Middle High German rüebe, Old High German ruoba, from Proto-West Germanic *rōbijā (compare Latin rāpa, Proto-Slavic *rěpa).

funFacts: Russian репа (repa), the turnip of the folk tale Репка (“The Enormous Turnip”), is compared with Latin rāpa and German Rübe.
In Switzerland children carve turnips (Räben) into lanterns for the Räbeliechtli processions in November.
pitfalls: Do not confuse with Steckrübe (rutabaga, yellow flesh) or Rote Bete (beetroot); Rübe alone is a vague cover term.
subtleties: Speise- (“food”) distinguishes it from Futterrüben (fodder beets) and Zuckerrüben (sugar beets).

profile.feeling: Pale, crisp, slightly bitter leaves – a winter salad from Belgium.

senses.def: chicory, Belgian endive (Cichorium intybus var. foliosum; the pale leaf buds)

examples.text: Chicorée schmeckt leicht bitter.
examples.tr: Chicory tastes slightly bitter.

examples.text: Den Chicorée halbieren und den bitteren Strunk herausschneiden.
examples.tr: Halve the chicory and cut out the bitter core.

examples.text: Chicorée wächst im Dunkeln, deshalb sind die Blätter fast weiß.
examples.tr: Chicory grows in the dark, which is why the leaves are almost white.

etymology.text: Borrowed from French chicorée (“chicory”), from Latin cichōrium, from Ancient Greek κιχώριον (kikhṓrion). Doublet of Zichorie.

funFacts: Chicory was first grown this way in Belgium in the 19th century; in Belgium and the Netherlands it is called witloof (“white leaf”).
pitfalls: Gender varies: der or die Chicorée (Wiktionary lists both). No plural: say zwei Stück Chicorée.
Pronounced the French way: SCHI-ko-ree; the germanized spelling Schikoree is rare.
subtleties: Its doublet Zichorie is the same species but usually means the root used for coffee substitute (Zichorienkaffee).

profile.feeling: Juicy, slightly sour summer leaves – a weed in the garden, a salad in Greece and Turkey.

senses.def: purslane (Portulaca oleracea, eaten as a salad green)

examples.text: Portulak schmeckt frisch und leicht säuerlich.
examples.tr: Purslane tastes fresh and slightly sour.

examples.text: In Griechenland isst man Portulak gern im Salat mit Tomaten und Feta.
examples.tr: In Greece people like to eat purslane in a salad with tomatoes and feta.

examples.text: Im Garten wächst der Portulak oft als Unkraut zwischen den Platten.
examples.tr: In the garden purslane often grows as a weed between the paving stones.

profile.synonymsNone: No current synonym; the older borrowing Burzel has been largely displaced (Wiktionary).

etymology.text: Borrowed on the verge of Middle High German to Early New High German from Latin portulaca; it largely displaced the earlier borrowing Burzel.

funFacts: Purslane is γλιστρίδα (glistrída) in Greek and semizotu in Turkish – both popular in summer salads.
pitfalls: The plural Portulake is rare; as a salad green it is uncountable.
subtleties: For a leafy vegetable it is unusually rich in omega-3 fatty acids, which made it popular in health food.

profile.feeling: Knobbly tubers with a nutty taste; organic markets and rustic winter cooking.

senses.def: Jerusalem artichoke, sunchoke (Helianthus tuberosus and its tubers)

examples.text: Topinambur schmeckt leicht nussig, ein bisschen wie Artischocke.
examples.tr: Jerusalem artichoke tastes slightly nutty, a little like artichoke.

examples.text: Wir haben Topinambur im Garten, und er breitet sich überall aus.
examples.tr: We have Jerusalem artichokes in the garden, and they spread everywhere.

examples.text: Aus Topinamburen kann man eine cremige Suppe kochen.
examples.tr: You can make a creamy soup from Jerusalem artichokes.

etymology.text: Borrowed from French topinambour.

funFacts: The French name topinambour comes from the Tupinambá, a people of Brazil, although the plant is from North America.
The English name is misleading: the tuber has nothing to do with Jerusalem and is not an artichoke.
pitfalls: Gender varies: der or die Topinambur (Wiktionary lists both). Plural Topinamburen.
subtleties: The plant is a sunflower (Helianthus); its yellow flowers look like small sunflowers.

profile.feeling: The burning sting on bare legs – and, for foragers, a free spring vegetable and tea.

senses.def: stinging nettle (Urtica dioica); its young leaves are eaten as greens
Chinese burn (twisting the skin of someone’s forearm)

examples.text: Junge Brennnesseln kann man wie Spinat kochen.
examples.tr: You can cook young nettles like spinach.

examples.text: Au! Ich habe in die Brennnesseln gefasst.
examples.tr: Ouch! I touched the nettles.

examples.text: Brennnesseltee ist ein altes Hausmittel.
examples.tr: Nettle tea is an old home remedy.

phrases.tr: to sit down in the nettles
phrases.meaning: to get oneself into trouble, to put one’s foot in it

synonyms.nuance: the shorter, more general word for any nettle; frequent in compounds

etymology.text: From brennen (“to burn”) + Nessel (“nettle”); Nessel is from Old High German neȥȥila, cognate with English nettle and Dutch netel.

funFacts: In the old spelling the word was written Brennessel; the reform of 1996 restored all three n.
pitfalls: Three n in a row: Brenn + Nessel = Brennnessel (spelling since the 1996 reform; before: Brennessel).
Wear gloves when picking; blanching or drying removes the sting.
subtleties: German Nesselsucht (hives, urticaria) and Latin Urtica both take their name from the nettle’s sting.

profile.feeling: The garlicky smell of spring woods; pesto and foraging trips in March and April.

senses.def: wild garlic, ramsons (Allium ursinum)

examples.text: Im März und April riecht der ganze Wald nach Bärlauch.
examples.tr: In March and April the whole forest smells of wild garlic.

examples.text: Aus Bärlauch, Öl und Parmesan mache ich ein Pesto.
examples.tr: I make a pesto from wild garlic, oil and parmesan.

examples.text: Wer Bärlauch sammelt, muss ihn gut von Maiglöckchen unterscheiden.
examples.tr: Anyone who gathers wild garlic must tell it apart carefully from lily of the valley.

synonyms.nuance: old regional name, related to English ramsons

etymology.text: From Bär (“bear”) + Lauch (“leek”). Calque of Latin Allium ursīnum (literally “bear garlic”).

funFacts: A popular story says bears eat it after their winter sleep – hence “bear leek”.
pitfalls: Dangerous look-alikes: Maiglöckchen (lily of the valley) and Herbstzeitlose (autumn crocus) are poisonous. Only Bärlauch smells of garlic when you rub a leaf.
Normally uncountable: Ich sammle Bärlauch.
subtleties: Unlike Knoblauch, you eat the leaves, not the bulb.

profile.feeling: Sweet, nutty winter root, rediscovered in soups and purées.

senses.def: parsnip (Pastinaca sativa and its root)

examples.text: Pastinaken schmecken süß und leicht nussig.
examples.tr: Parsnips taste sweet and slightly nutty.

examples.text: Die Pastinake sieht aus wie eine weiße Karotte.
examples.tr: The parsnip looks like a white carrot.

examples.text: Im Winter mache ich Püree aus Pastinaken und Kartoffeln.
examples.tr: In winter I make a purée of parsnips and potatoes.

profile.synonymsNone: No current synonym; Pastinak and Pasternake are archaic forms (Wiktionary).

etymology.text: From Middle High German pasternacke, from Old High German pastinaka, from Proto-West Germanic *pastinakā (“parsnip”).

funFacts: Russian пастернак (pasternak) means parsnip – it is the surname of the writer Boris Pasternak.
pitfalls: Do not confuse with Petersilienwurzel (root parsley), which looks very similar but is smaller and tastes of parsley.
subtleties: Its sweetness increases after frost, so it is a typical winter vegetable.

profile.feeling: Lemony sour leaves chewed in meadows as a child; Frankfurt green sauce.

senses.def: sorrel (Rumex acetosa), a sour leafy herb

examples.text: Sauerampfer schmeckt sauer, fast wie Zitrone.
examples.tr: Sorrel tastes sour, almost like lemon.

examples.text: Für die Frankfurter Grüne Soße braucht man auch Sauerampfer.
examples.tr: For Frankfurt green sauce you also need sorrel.

examples.text: Als Kinder haben wir auf der Wiese Sauerampfer gekaut.
examples.tr: As children we chewed sorrel in the meadow.

synonyms.nuance: the genus Rumex in general, including inedible docks

etymology.text: sauer (“sour, acidic”) + Ampfer (“sorrel”); Ampfer is from Old High German ampfaro, an adjective (“sharp, bitter”) used as a noun.

funFacts: In Russia and Ukraine sorrel (щавель) makes a sour green soup, зелёный борщ (green borscht).
pitfalls: Do not eat large amounts: the sour taste comes from oxalic acid (Oxalsäure).
The plural is the same as the singular; the herb itself is uncountable.
subtleties: sauer + Ampfer doubles the idea: Ampfer itself originally meant “sour, bitter” (Wiktionary calls it a tautological compound).

profile.feeling: Sharp enough to make your eyes water: with smoked fish, boiled beef and sausages.

senses.def: horseradish (Armoracia rusticana and its pungent root)
horseradish as a condiment or sauce (grated, often with cream)

examples.text: Beim Reiben von Meerrettich tränen einem die Augen.
examples.tr: Your eyes water when you grate horseradish.

examples.text: Zur geräucherten Forelle passt Sahnemeerrettich sehr gut.
examples.tr: Creamed horseradish goes very well with smoked trout.

examples.text: In Österreich sagt man zum Meerrettich Kren.
examples.tr: In Austria horseradish is called Kren.

synonyms.nuance: the usual word in Austria and Bavaria (der Kren)

etymology.text: From Middle High German merretich, from Old High German meriratih; by surface analysis Meer (“sea”) + Rettich (“radish”), with Meer in the old sense “foreign” (as in Meerkatze, Meerschweinchen). Explanations from mehr (“more”) or Mähre (“mare”) are not supported by the old spellings.

funFacts: The Austrian Kren comes from a Slavic word: Russian хрен (khren) and Czech křen are its relatives.
At the Jewish Passover Seder, horseradish often serves as the bitter herb (maror), in Hebrew חֲזֶרֶת (ḥazeret).
pitfalls: Meer here does not mean “sea” in the usual sense; the horseradish has nothing to do with the sea.
Plural Meerrettiche (several roots); as a condiment it is uncountable.
subtleties: The sharpness comes from mustard oils released only when the root is grated, so it is grated just before serving.

profile.feeling: Hearty northern winter stews – and a memory of hunger in the First World War.

senses.def: rutabaga, swede (Brassica napus var. napobrassica)

examples.text: Steckrüben haben gelbes Fruchtfleisch und schmecken leicht süß.
examples.tr: Swedes have yellow flesh and taste slightly sweet.

examples.text: Im Steckrübenwinter 1916/17 aßen viele Deutsche fast nur Steckrüben.
examples.tr: In the “turnip winter” of 1916/17 many Germans ate almost nothing but swedes.

examples.text: Steckrübeneintopf ist ein typisches Wintergericht in Norddeutschland.
examples.tr: Swede stew is a typical winter dish in northern Germany.

synonyms.nuance: the same vegetable; in Austria it can also mean kohlrabi
used in Berlin, Brandenburg and the north-east

etymology.text: From stecken (“to stick, insert”) + Rübe (“turnip, root vegetable”).

funFacts: English swede is short for “Swedish turnip”.
pitfalls: Not the same as Speiserübe (turnip, white flesh): the Steckrübe is larger, with yellow flesh.
In Austria Kohlrübe can also mean kohlrabi.
subtleties: Because of the wartime “turnip winter”, the Steckrübe was long seen as poor people’s food; today it is back in regional cooking.

profile.feeling: Peppery green leaves from clear, cold springs.

senses.def: watercress (Nasturtium officinale)

examples.text: Brunnenkresse wächst in sauberen Bächen und Quellen.
examples.tr: Watercress grows in clean streams and springs.

examples.text: Brunnenkresse schmeckt pfeffrig und scharf.
examples.tr: Watercress tastes peppery and hot.

examples.text: Ich streue Brunnenkresse über die Kartoffelsuppe.
examples.tr: I sprinkle watercress over the potato soup.

etymology.text: From Brunnen (“well, spring”) + Kresse (“cress”).

funFacts: Brunnen originally meant a spring, not only a dug well – hence “spring cress”.
pitfalls: Do not pick it from stagnant or polluted water: it can carry parasites such as the liver fluke.
Usually uncountable; the plural Brunnenkressen is rare.
subtleties: Kresse alone usually means garden cress (veg.cress); for watercress say Brunnenkresse.

profile.feeling: Tiny green sprouts on a windowsill, egg sandwiches and children’s first gardening.

senses.def: garden cress (Lepidium sativum), usually eaten as young sprouts

examples.text: Die Kinder säen Kresse auf feuchter Watte.
examples.tr: The children sow cress on damp cotton wool.

examples.text: Ein Brot mit Ei und Kresse ist schnell gemacht.
examples.tr: A slice of bread with egg and cress is quickly made.

examples.text: Nach einer Woche kannst du die Kresse schon ernten.
examples.tr: After a week you can already harvest the cress.

synonyms.nuance: the full name of the plant, distinguishing it from Brunnenkresse (watercress)

etymology.text: From Middle High German kresse, from Old High German kressa, from Proto-West Germanic *krassjā. Cognate with English cress.

funFacts: Cress grows so fast that sowing it is a classic first growing experiment for children.
pitfalls: Normally uncountable; the plural Kressen is used only for kinds of cress.
subtleties: In German Kresse usually means the small seedlings sold in trays and cut with scissors; Brunnenkresse is watercress.

profile.feeling: Asian stir-fries: long hollow stems with garlic and chilli.

senses.def: water spinach, morning glory greens (Ipomoea aquatica)

examples.text: Wasserspinat hat hohle Stängel.
examples.tr: Water spinach has hollow stems.

examples.text: Im Thai-Restaurant bestelle ich gebratenen Wasserspinat mit Knoblauch.
examples.tr: At the Thai restaurant I order stir-fried water spinach with garlic.

examples.text: Den Wasserspinat nur kurz im Wok braten, sonst wird er matschig.
examples.tr: Only stir-fry the water spinach briefly in the wok, otherwise it gets mushy.

profile.synonymsNone: No established German synonym; Asian shops also use names such as Kangkong.

etymology.text: Wasser (“water”) + Spinat (“spinach”); Spinat is borrowed from Italian spinace.

funFacts: Chinese calls it 空心菜 (kōngxīncài), “hollow-heart vegetable”, because of its hollow stems.
pitfalls: It is not a kind of spinach: it is related to the sweet potato (genus Ipomoea).
Masculine like Spinat (der Wasserspinat); no plural.
subtleties: The word is mostly used in Asian restaurants and shops; most Germans do not know the vegetable.

profile.feeling: Fine French cooking: small, mild, aromatic onions for sauces.

senses.def: shallot

examples.text: Für die Soße hacke ich zwei Schalotten ganz fein.
examples.tr: For the sauce I chop two shallots very finely.

examples.text: Schalotten sind milder als normale Zwiebeln.
examples.tr: Shallots are milder than ordinary onions.

examples.text: Auf dem Markt kauft er ein Netz Schalotten.
examples.tr: At the market he buys a net of shallots.

synonyms.nuance: old German name (Wiktionary), no longer in everyday use

etymology.text: Borrowed from French échalote.

funFacts: French échalote goes back to Latin (cēpa) Ascalōnia, “onion from Ascalon” – the city of Ashkelon (Hebrew אַשְׁקְלוֹן) on the coast of Israel.
pitfalls: Stress on the second syllable: Scha-LOT-te. Plural Schalotten.
subtleties: Shallots grow in clusters of several bulbs, unlike a single onion.

profile.feeling: Tropical staple from West Africa, Asia and the Caribbean; often confused with sweet potato.

senses.def: yam (tubers of Dioscorea species)

examples.text: In Westafrika ist die Yamswurzel ein wichtiges Grundnahrungsmittel.
examples.tr: In West Africa the yam is an important staple food.

examples.text: Die Yamswurzel ist keine Süßkartoffel, auch wenn man sie oft verwechselt.
examples.tr: The yam is not a sweet potato, even though people often mix them up.

examples.text: In Nigeria isst man gern gestampfte Yamswurzel.
examples.tr: In Nigeria people like to eat pounded yam.

synonyms.nuance: shorter name, also used for the plant

etymology.text: Yams- (compare English yam, borrowed from Portuguese inhame and Spanish ñame, likely from Wolof ñàmbi) + Wurzel (“root”).

funFacts: In the USA orange sweet potatoes are often sold as “yams”, which adds to the confusion.
pitfalls: Feminine because of Wurzel: die Yamswurzel, plural die Yamswurzeln.
subtleties: Botanically it is a tuber of Dioscorea, unrelated to the sweet potato (Ipomoea) and the potato.

profile.feeling: Big green leaves with colourful stalks – a cousin of spinach in the garden and the pan.

senses.def: Swiss chard, chard (Beta vulgaris var. cicla)

examples.text: Mangold hat große Blätter und dicke, oft bunte Stiele.
examples.tr: Chard has big leaves and thick, often colourful stalks.

examples.text: Die Stiele vom Mangold kochst du etwas länger als die Blätter.
examples.tr: You cook the chard stalks a little longer than the leaves.

examples.text: Mangold ist mit der Roten Bete verwandt.
examples.tr: Chard is related to beetroot.

synonyms.nuance: the type grown for its thick stalks

etymology.text: From Middle High German man(e)golt. Further origin unknown.

funFacts: Arabic calls chard سِلْق (silq); Turkish says pazı.
pitfalls: The plural Mangolde is rare; normally uncountable: Ich kaufe Mangold.
Mangold is also a German surname, unrelated in meaning.
subtleties: It is the same species as beetroot and sugar beet (Beta vulgaris), but grown for its leaves and stalks.

profile.feeling: Crunchy strips in Chinese dishes, mostly from a tin.

senses.def: bamboo shoot (the edible young shoot of bamboo)

examples.text: Bambussprossen kaufe ich meistens aus der Dose.
examples.tr: I mostly buy bamboo shoots in a tin.

examples.text: Frische Bambussprossen muss man vor dem Essen kochen.
examples.tr: Fresh bamboo shoots must be cooked before eating.

examples.text: In der Suppe sind Pilze, Tofu und Bambussprossen.
examples.tr: There are mushrooms, tofu and bamboo shoots in the soup.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; the word is almost always used in the plural (Bambussprossen).

etymology.text: Bambus (“bamboo”) + Sprosse (“sprout”). Bambus came via early modern Dutch bamboes and Portuguese bambu from Malay bambu, from Kannada bambu.

funFacts: Chinese 竹笋 (zhúsǔn): the character 笋 has the bamboo radical ⺮ on top.
pitfalls: Feminine: die Bambussprosse, because die Sprosse is feminine; plural Bambussprossen (the usual form).
Raw bamboo shoots contain toxic substances; fresh ones must be cooked well.
subtleties: Do not confuse die Sprosse (sprout; also rung of a ladder) with der Spross (shoot of a plant; also “offspring”).

profile.feeling: Italian cooking, pizza and modern salads; peppery and nutty.

senses.def: arugula, rocket (Eruca sativa)

examples.text: Auf die Pizza kommen erst nach dem Backen Rucola und Parmesan.
examples.tr: Rocket and parmesan go on the pizza only after baking.

examples.text: Rucola schmeckt nussig und leicht scharf.
examples.tr: Rocket tastes nutty and slightly hot.

examples.text: In den 1990er-Jahren wurde Rucola in Deutschland plötzlich modern.
examples.tr: In the 1990s rocket suddenly became fashionable in Germany.

synonyms.nuance: the older German name, used in botany and by some cooks

etymology.text: Borrowed from Italian rucola, diminutive of ruca, whence already earlier German Rauke. Eventually from Latin ērūca.

funFacts: Greek ρόκα, Turkish roka and Arabic جَرْجِير (jarjīr) all name the same salad plant.
pitfalls: No plural: Rucola is uncountable. Feminine in Wiktionary: die Rucola.
subtleties: Rucola sounds modern and Mediterranean; the older German name Rauke sounds botanical or old-fashioned.

profile.feeling: The classic German winter salad: small dark-green rosettes with bacon and croutons.

senses.def: lamb’s lettuce, corn salad (Valerianella locusta)

examples.text: Feldsalat ist ein typischer Wintersalat.
examples.tr: Lamb’s lettuce is a typical winter salad.

examples.text: Den Feldsalat musst du gut waschen, weil oft Erde zwischen den Blättern ist.
examples.tr: You have to wash the lamb’s lettuce well, because there is often soil between the leaves.

examples.text: Feldsalat heißt in Österreich Vogerlsalat und in der Schweiz Nüsslisalat.
examples.tr: Lamb’s lettuce is called Vogerlsalat in Austria and Nüsslisalat in Switzerland.

synonyms.nuance: regional name, best known from the fairy tale

etymology.text: Feld (“field”) + Salat (“lettuce, salad”).

funFacts: The fairy-tale heroine Rapunzel is named after the plant her mother craved: Rapunzel is a regional name for lamb’s lettuce (and for rampion).
pitfalls: The plural Feldsalate is rare; normally uncountable.
subtleties: Wiktionary lists about twenty regional names – Feldsalat is a showcase of German regional vocabulary.

profile.feeling: Flat green leaves that look like chives and smell of garlic; Chinese dumplings.

senses.def: garlic chives, Chinese chives (Allium tuberosum)

examples.text: Schnittknoblauch sieht aus wie Schnittlauch, schmeckt aber nach Knoblauch.
examples.tr: Garlic chives look like chives but taste of garlic.

examples.text: Für die Teigtaschen hacke ich Schnittknoblauch und Ei.
examples.tr: For the dumplings I chop garlic chives and egg.

examples.text: Schnittknoblauch wächst gut im Kräuterbeet.
examples.tr: Garlic chives grow well in the herb bed.

synonyms.nuance: name used in Asian shops and recipes

etymology.text: Schnitt (“cut”) + Knoblauch (“garlic”).

funFacts: In Chinese it is 韭菜 (jiǔcài), a classic dumpling (饺子) filling with egg or pork.
pitfalls: No plural; masculine like Knoblauch.
subtleties: Its leaves are flat, while those of Schnittlauch (chives) are hollow tubes.

profile.feeling: Old-fashioned winter vegetable: black, sticky roots and a mild asparagus-like taste.

senses.def: black salsify, scorzonera (Scorzonera hispanica)

examples.text: Schwarzwurzeln nennt man auch Winterspargel.
examples.tr: Black salsify is also called winter asparagus.

examples.text: Beim Schälen der Schwarzwurzeln trage ich Handschuhe, weil der Saft klebt.
examples.tr: When peeling black salsify I wear gloves because the sap is sticky.

examples.text: Schwarzwurzeln in Rahmsoße sind ein altes Wintergericht.
examples.tr: Black salsify in cream sauce is an old winter dish.

synonyms.nuance: nickname: a winter vegetable that tastes a little like asparagus

etymology.text: From schwarz (“black”) + Wurzel (“root”).

funFacts: The black skin hides a pure white root – hence the name “black root”.
pitfalls: Feminine because of Wurzel; plural Schwarzwurzeln (mostly used in the plural).
subtleties: Peeled roots turn brown quickly, so cooks put them into water with vinegar or lemon juice.

profile.feeling: Bavarian beer gardens: thin spirals of salted white radish with pretzels.

senses.def: radish, especially the large white radish (daikon)

examples.text: Im Biergarten gibt es Brezen, Obatzda und Rettich.
examples.tr: In the beer garden there are pretzels, Obatzda and white radish.

examples.text: Der Rettich wird in dünne Spiralen geschnitten und gesalzen.
examples.tr: The radish is cut into thin spirals and salted.

examples.text: Japanischer Rettich heißt Daikon und ist lang und weiß.
examples.tr: Japanese radish is called daikon and is long and white.

synonyms.nuance: the Japanese name, used for the long white East Asian radish

etymology.text: From Middle High German retich, from Old High German retich, rātih, from Proto-West Germanic *radik, *rādik. Doublet of Radix.

funFacts: Japanese 大根 (daikon) means “big root”; Chinese calls it 萝卜 (luóbo).
Rettich and Radieschen both go back to Latin rādīx (“root”).
pitfalls: Rettich is the big radish; the small red one is das Radieschen (veg.1).
Plural Rettiche, dative plural Rettichen.
subtleties: Bavarians salt the slices so that the Radi “weeps” (gives off water) before eating; this takes away some of the sharpness.

profile.feeling: Ugly outside, aromatic inside: soup greens, celeriac salad and breaded celeriac “schnitzel”.

senses.def: celeriac, celery root

examples.text: Für die Brühe braucht man Karotten, Lauch und Knollensellerie.
examples.tr: For the broth you need carrots, leek and celeriac.

examples.text: Knollensellerie kann man in Scheiben braten wie ein Schnitzel.
examples.tr: You can fry celeriac in slices like a schnitzel.

examples.text: Der Knollensellerie ist außen hässlich, aber innen weiß und aromatisch.
examples.tr: Celeriac is ugly outside but white and aromatic inside.

synonyms.nuance: the general word; in Germany it usually means celeriac

etymology.text: Knolle (“tuber”) + -n- + Sellerie; Sellerie is borrowed from French céleri, from Lombard selleri, from Latin selīnum, from Ancient Greek σέλῑνον (sélīnon).

funFacts: Suppengrün, the bunch of soup vegetables sold in Germany, usually contains carrot, leek, parsley and a piece of celeriac.
pitfalls: Gender varies: der or die Knollensellerie (Wiktionary lists both); in Austria and the south die Sellerie is common.
In Germany plain Sellerie usually means this root, not the stalks.
subtleties: Same species as Staudensellerie (veg.1), but grown for the round root.

profile.feeling: Long crisp leaves – Caesar salad and grilled lettuce hearts.

senses.def: romaine lettuce, cos

examples.text: Für einen Caesar Salad nimmt man Römersalat.
examples.tr: For a Caesar salad you use romaine lettuce.

examples.text: Römersalat hat lange, feste Blätter.
examples.tr: Romaine lettuce has long, firm leaves.

examples.text: Ich kaufe zwei Köpfe Römersalat.
examples.tr: I am buying two heads of romaine lettuce.

synonyms.nuance: traditional name; the heads were once tied together to keep the heart pale

etymology.text: Römer (“Roman”) + Salat (“lettuce”).

funFacts: In Greece this type of lettuce is the everyday salad leaf, μαρούλι (marouli).
Hebrew חַסָּה (ḥassa) and Arabic خَسّ (khass), both “lettuce”, are related Semitic words.
pitfalls: Several heads: zwei Römersalate or, more often, zwei Köpfe Römersalat.
subtleties: Caesar salad is named after the restaurateur Caesar Cardini, not after the Romans – but Römersalat really means “Roman lettuce”.

profile.feeling: Italian elegance: wine-red, bitter leaves with white veins.

senses.def: radicchio (red-leaved Italian chicory)

examples.text: Radicchio schmeckt bitter und hat rote Blätter mit weißen Adern.
examples.tr: Radicchio tastes bitter and has red leaves with white veins.

examples.text: Der Radicchio aus Treviso hat lange, schmale Blätter.
examples.tr: Radicchio from Treviso has long, narrow leaves.

examples.text: Ein bisschen Radicchio macht den grünen Salat bunter.
examples.tr: A little radicchio makes the green salad more colourful.

profile.synonymsNone: No German synonym: the Italian name is used; botanically it is a kind of Zichorie (chicory).

etymology.text: Borrowed from Italian radicchio, from Latin rādīcula (“little root”), diminutive of rādīx.

funFacts: Italian radicchio, German Rettich and Radieschen all go back to Latin rādīx (“root”).
pitfalls: Pronounced the Italian way: ra-DIK-kjo – cch is a k sound.
Masculine (der Radicchio); Duden gives the genitive des Radicchio or des Radicchios and no plural.
subtleties: It belongs to the same species as Chicorée (Cichorium intybus).

profile.feeling: Mild purple rings in Greek salad and on burgers; pink pickled onions.

senses.def: red onion

examples.text: Rote Zwiebeln sind milder als gelbe und passen gut in Salate.
examples.tr: Red onions are milder than yellow ones and go well in salads.

examples.text: Für den griechischen Salat schneide ich eine rote Zwiebel in Ringe.
examples.tr: For the Greek salad I cut a red onion into rings.

examples.text: Eingelegte rote Zwiebeln werden schön pink.
examples.tr: Pickled red onions turn a lovely pink.

profile.synonymsNone: No other word: rote Zwiebel is an adjective + noun description (product names sometimes write Rote Zwiebel).

etymology.text: rot (“red”) + Zwiebel (“onion”); Zwiebel is from Middle High German zwibel, Old High German zwibollo, from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

funFacts: The colour comes from anthocyanins, the same pigments as in red cabbage.
The Tropea onion from Calabria is Italy’s most famous red onion.
pitfalls: rote is an adjective and is declined: die rote Zwiebel, eine rote Zwiebel, mit der roten Zwiebel, die roten Zwiebeln, but rote Zwiebeln without an article.
Written with a small r: it is a normal description, not a fixed name like Rote Bete.
subtleties: Because it is a free combination, you can also say die Zwiebel ist rot; only the noun Zwiebel is a dictionary word.

profile.feeling: Crunchy and watery: burgers, kebabs and canteen salads.

senses.def: iceberg lettuce

examples.text: Eisbergsalat ist knackig, schmeckt aber nach fast nichts.
examples.tr: Iceberg lettuce is crunchy but tastes of almost nothing.

examples.text: Auf den Burger kommen Tomate, Gurke und Eisbergsalat.
examples.tr: Tomato, cucumber and iceberg lettuce go on the burger.

examples.text: Ein Kopf Eisbergsalat hält sich im Kühlschrank lange.
examples.tr: A head of iceberg lettuce keeps for a long time in the fridge.

etymology.text: Calque of English iceberg lettuce: Eisberg (“iceberg”) + Salat (“lettuce”).

funFacts: The name is said to come from the USA, where the lettuce was transported packed in crushed ice.
pitfalls: Plural Eisbergsalate means several heads; for the leaves use the uncountable singular.
subtleties: Salat means both “lettuce” and “salad (dish)”; Eisbergsalat is the lettuce, not a finished salad.

profile.feeling: Bitter, curly or broad green leaves – an old-fashioned autumn and winter salad.

senses.def: endive (Cichorium endivia: curly endive and escarole)

examples.text: Endivie schmeckt leicht bitter.
examples.tr: Endive tastes slightly bitter.

examples.text: Endivien untereinander ist ein altes Gericht aus Kartoffelpüree und Endivie.
examples.tr: “Endivien untereinander” is an old dish of mashed potato and endive.

examples.text: Die krause Endivie heißt im Laden oft Friséesalat.
examples.tr: Curly endive is often called frisée in the shop.

etymology.text: Via a Romance language (compare French endive, Italian indivia), from Late Latin intibus.

funFacts: The dish Endivien untereinander (endive mixed into mashed potatoes) is a traditional dish in the west of Germany.
pitfalls: Plural Endivien; four syllables: En-di-vi-e.
False friend: American English “Belgian endive” is Chicorée, not Endivie.
subtleties: Endivie, Chicorée and Radicchio are all bitter relatives in the genus Cichorium.

absent.reason: No established everyday German word: leaf mustard (Brassica juncea) is hardly used in German cooking, and Wiktionary has no German entry for it.
absent.use: Blattsenf (gardening) or Sareptasenf (botany); in Asian shops the Chinese or Japanese names, or English “mustard greens”.

absent.reason: No German word in common use: jute mallow is known only from Arab and African cooking.
absent.use: The Arabic name Molokhia / Mulukhiya (from مُلُوخِيَّة), or the botanical Langkapseljute or Gemüsejute.
